also: as bad luck would have it

terms.grammar: phrase: accidit with the adverb, and a quod-clause for what happened
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.17.2: sed accidit perincommodē quod eum nusquam vīdistī
terms.comment: Latin says that a thing turned out badly where English comments on it with an adverb. Perincommodē is “very unfortunately”. Incommodē alone is “inconveniently, at a bad moment” (Lewis & Short), and nōn incommodē is “quite conveniently”.
Stronger than incommodē: of what ends in misfortune, a plan tried and failed.

terms.gloss: I wish it weren’t so; I’m sorry (that)
terms.grammar: imperfect subjunctive of nōlō, with an accusative or a perfect participle
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.35 (Lewis & Short): Carthāginem et Numantiam funditus sustulērunt; nōllem Corinthum
terms.comment: The speaker’s regret as a wish: nōllem factum, “I wish it hadn’t happened”, Terence’s stock apology. For a sigh of grief, heu (see alas).

phrases.latin: sed accidit perincommodē quod eum nusquam vīdistī.
phrases.english: But unfortunately you never saw him anywhere.
That’s bad luck. — No, it’s a disaster.

phrases.latin: Nōvī ego vestra haec: «Nōllem factum»; jūsjūrandum dabitur tē esse indignum injūriā hāc
phrases.english: I know your sort: “I’m sorry it happened”; you’ll swear you never deserved such treatment
